title-group.article-title: Cell signalling pathways for the regulation of GATA4 transcription factor: Implications for cell growth and apoptosis

abstract.p: GATA4 is a member of the GATA family of zinc finger transcription factor, which regulates gene transcription by binding to GATA elements. GATA4 was originally discovered as a regulator of cardiac development and subsequently identified as a major regulator of adult cardiac hypertrophy. GATA4 regulate gene expression of various genes, which are involved in cardiac development and cardiac hypertrophy and heart failure. In addition to the heart, GATA4 plays important roles in the reproductive system, gastrointestinal system, respiratory system and cancer. Positive and negative regulations of GATA4 therefore are important components of biologic functions. The activation of GATA4 occurs via various cell signaling events. Earlier studies have identified protein-protein interactions of GATA4 with other factors. The discovery of interactions of GATA4 with nuclear factor for activated T cells (NFAT) revealed the importance of calcium signaling in the activation of GATA4. GATA4 can also be phosphorylated by mitogen activated protein kinases and protein kinase A. Lysine modifications also occur on the GATA4 molecule including acetylation and sumoylation. Both reactive oxygen-dependent and –independent antioxidant-sensitive pathways for GATA4 activation have also been demonstrated. The GATA4 activity is also regulated by modulating the level of GATA4 expression via transcriptional as well as translational mechanisms. This work summarizes the current understanding of regulatory mechanisms for modulating GATA4 activity.

sec.title: GATA4 AS A REGULATOR OF CELL GROWTH AND DEATH
sec.p: Various genes contain GATA binding sequences including the consensus 5′-WGATAR-3′ sequence, where W is A or T and R is A or G (Evans, 1988 [1]; Orkin, 1992 [2]). Binding of transcription factors to these GATA elements regulates a variety of biological processes. Six members of the GATA family of zinc finger transcription factors have been identified, and are named GATA-1, -2, -3, -4, -5 and -6 (Molkentin, 2000 [3]).

GATA4 was initially discovered as a regulator of cardiac development (Kelley et al., 1993 [4]; Arceci et al., 1993 [5]). GATA4 was then found to play essential roles in the development of clinically important cardiac hypertrophy (Molkentin & Olson, 1997 [6]) by activating the expression of genes such as angiotensin II type1a receptor (Herzig et al., 1997 [7]) and beta-myosin heavy chain (Hasegawa et al., 1997 [8]) in response to pressure overload to the left ventricle. A number of other proteins that are important for cardiac hypertrophy such as alpha-myosin heavy chain (Molkentin et al., 1994 [9]), myosin light chains (McGrew et al., 1996 [10]), troponin C (Ip et al., 1994 [11]), troponin I (Murphy et al., 1997 [12]), troponin C (Montgomery & Litvin, 1997 [13]), Na+-Ca2+ exchanger (Nicholas & Philipson, 1999 [14]; Cheng et al., 1999 [15]), atrial natriuretic factor (Durocher et al., 1997 [16]), and brain natriuretic factor (Thuerauf et al., 1994 [17]) also contain GATA regulatory sites in their promoters. Further, various hypertrophic stimuli such as alpha-adrenergic agonist and endothelin-1 were found to activate GATA-4 in cardiomyocytes (Morimoto et al., 2000 [18]; Hautala et al., 2001 [19]). In transgenic mice overexpressing calsequestrin with cardiac hypertrophy (Jones et al., 1998 [20]), GATA4 was found to be activated in the heart (Suzuki et al., 1999 [21]).

In addition to established roles of GATA4 in cardiac hypertrophy, GATA4 also regulates cell survival (anti-apoptotic) signaling. Evidence for the role of GATA factors in the regulation of apoptosis was initially generated in the studies of GATA1 deficient precursors that were found to undergo apoptosis (Weiss and Orkin, 1995 [22]). Further, apoptosis induced by estrogen was associated with the inhibition of GATA1 in erythroleukemia cells (Blobel et al., 1995 [23]; Blobel & Orkin, 1996 [24]). Gregory et al. (1999 [25]) also reported that GATA1 induced the expression of anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-xL. The bcl-x gene generates five Bcl-x isoforms including Bcl-xL, Bcl-xS, Bcl-xβ, Bcl-xγ and Bcl-xΔTM from different splicing protein products (Pecci et al., 2001 [26]). Bcl-xL (233 amino acids) is anti-apoptotic and shorter Bcl-xS (170 amino acids) is a dominant negative repressor of Bcl-xL and Bcl-2 (Minn et al., 1996 [27]; Boise et al., 1993 [28]; Sorenson, 2004 [29]). These protein isoforms are translated from different mRNAs that are regulated by various regions within the bcl-x gene promoter. The proximal promoter region located within 802 bp upstream from the ATG site is responsible for the regulation of Bcl-xL gene expression (Pecci et al., 2001 [26]). These regions of the bcl-x promoter are conserved among species with various putative regulatory cis-elements including two GATA elements (Grillot et al., 1997 [30]). More recent reports suggest that the mechanism of GATA1-mediated upregulation of Bcl-xL involves protein phosphorylation (Yu et al., 2005 [31]) as well as the regulation by Gfi-1B (Kuo & Chang, 2007 [32]). Another anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2 has also been shown to be regulated by GATA1 (Tanaka et al., 2000 [33]). Recently, GATA3 was also found to upregulate Bcl-xL expression in osteoblasts (Chen et al., 2010 [35]).

GATA4 was also found to regulate apoptosis, as ovarian cell apoptosis was found to be associated with decreased expression of GATA4 (Heikinheimo et al., 1997 [35]; Vaskivuo et al., 2001 [36]). Also, cardiogenesis is enhanced in embryonic stem cells overexpressing GATA4, and the depletion of GATA4 results in apoptosis (Grepin et al., 1997 [37]). In adult cardiac myocytes, Kakita et al (2001 [38]) reported that the calcineurin/NFAT/GATA4 pathway is required for endothelin-1 mediated protection against cardiac myocyte apoptosis. Our laboratory has shown that the overexpression of GATA4 prevented cardiac myocyte apoptosis induced by anthracyclines such as daunorubicin and doxorubicin (Kim et al., 2003 [39]). We also reported that hepatocyte growth factor with the cardiac muscle cell survival activity caused the activation of GATA4 through MEK/ERK-dependent phosphorylation and upregulated Bcl-xL expression (Kitta et al., 2003 [40]). Anthracyclines were also found to downregulate GATA4 expression, suggesting that the mechanism of apoptosis may involve the regulation of GATA4. Nemer and co-workers (Aries et al., 2004 [41]) also showed doxorubicin-mediated downregulation of GATA4 in the heart of intact mice. Anthracycline-mediated downregulation of GATA4 in cardiac muscle has subsequently been reported by a number of laboratories (Bien et al., 2007 [42]; Suliman et al., 2007 [43]; Esaki et al., 2008 [44]; Riad et al., 2008 [45]; Koka et al., 2010 [46]). Other apoptotic stimuli such as mercury (Suzuki, 2003 [47]) and ischemia/reperfusion (Suzuki et al., 2004 [48]) also downregulate GATA4 expression. Studies of genetically modified mice demonstrated that GATA4 knock-down induced cardiac myocyte apoptosis and heart failure (Oka et al., 2006 [49]; Bisping et al., 2006 [50]). In mice, intermittent hypoxia with the preconditioning activity promoted the activation of GATA4 and upregulated Bcl-xL expression (Park et al., 2007 [51]). Kobayashi et al. (2006 [52]) demonstrated that GATA4 also regulates Bcl-2 expression in cardiac myocytes. GATA4 was found to prevent apoptosis induced by depletion of alpha-adrenergic receptor signaling (Huang et al., 2008 [53]) and to play a role in cell survival induced by cardiotrophin-1 (He-nan et al., 2009 [54]). GATA4 is involved in erythropoietin-induced cardioprotection against ischemia/reperfusion injury in the mouse heart (Shan et al., 2009 [55]). Interestingly, GATA4 also serves as a survival factor in cancer cells by regulating the expression of anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 (Kyronlahti et al., 2008 [56]) and Bcl-xL (Jaaskelainen et al., 2010 [57]).

sec.title: REGULATION OF GATA4 ACTIVATION BY CALCIUM SIGNALING
sec.p: The activity of GATA4 can be increased and decreased by modulating the activity of the already existing GATA4 molecule through post-translational modifications or by increasing the expression of GATA4. Post-translational modification mechanisms include protein-protein interactions, protein phosphorylation, and lysine modifications.

GATA4 has been shown to interact with some regulatory proteins including dHAND, FOG2, GATA6, MEF2, Nkx2.5, p300, RXRα and SRF (Pikkarainen et al., 2004 [58]). Molkentin et al. (1998 [59]) discovered that GATA4 can interact with nuclear factor for activated T-cells (NFAT) in the heart. The discovery of NFAT-GATA4 interactions in the heart was surprising because, while NFAT has been well studied in immune cells, its activity in the heart or in any other muscular systems was unknown. NFAT is activated when it is dephosphorylated by a calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein phosphatase, calcineurin. The paper by Molkentin et al. (1998 [59]) published in Cell describes that the expression of a constitutively active mutant of calcinuerin promoted cardiac hypertrophy in mice. A subsequent report by the same group published in Science demonstrated that the treatment with a calcineurin inhibitor cyclosporine blocked the development of cardiac hypertrophy induced by pressure-overload or genetic manipulations (Sussman et al., 1998 [60]). These findings suggested that calcium signaling regulates the GATA4 activation. Consistent with these findings, we also demonstrated that activities of NFAT and GATA4 are enhanced in the heart of mice, which overexpress cardiac calsequestrin (Suzuki et al., 1999 [21]). Calsequestrin is the major calcium binding protein of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, the calcium storage site of srtirated muscles. Sarcoplasmic reticular calcium plays essential roles in excitation-contraction coupling and the discovery of calsequestrin (MacLennan & Wong, 1971 [61]; Ikemoto et al., 1972 [62]) indicated that calcium does not freely exist in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, but is tightly regulated by calcium-binding proteins. As calsequestin has high capacity for calcium binding, it was not surprising for us to observed that cardiac myocytes from calsequetrin overexpressing mice have increased calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum induced by caffeine which directly opens up the ryanodine receptor, suggesting that the sarcoplasmic reticulum is overloaded with calcium (Jones et al., 1998 [20]). Surprisingly, however, despite the increased calcium load, depolarization-dependent calcium-induced calcium released was suppressed with slow and sustained kinetics in these mice compared to cardiac myocytes from non-transgenic littermates (Jones et al., 1998 [20]). Moreover, these mice were found to exhibit cardiac hypertrophy (Jone et al., 1998 [20]). In light of findings in T-cells that slow and sustained calcium release can specifically activate the NFAT pathway (Dolmetsch et al., 1997 [63]), we hypothesized that slow and sustained kinetics of calcium release, which is distinct from normal contractile calcium exhibiting fast and transient kinetic of calcium release, may trigger the activation of calmodulin/calcineurin/NFAT/GATA4 pathway in cardiac myocytes and may promote cardiac hypertrophy (Morad & Suzuki, 2000 [64]). Consistent to this idea, the treatment of cardiac myocytes with hydrogen peroxide, which modulates the kinetics of ryanodine receptor-dependent calcium release (Goldhaber & Liu, 1994 [65]; Suzuki et al., 1998 [66]), allowed for depolarization-induced GATA4 activation (Morad & Suzuki, 2000 [64]). Fig. 1 summarizes the published findings concerning the role of calcium signaling in GATA4 activation.

Consistent to the idea that calcium regulates GATA4 activation and cardiac hypertrophy, Morimoto et al. (2001; [67]) reported that norepinephrine-induced stimulation of endothelin-1 expression in cardiac myocytes is mediated by calcium-activated calcineurin-NFAT-GATA4 pathway. It is interesting to note that calcium also regulates the translational control of GATA4 mRNA (Sharma et al., 2007 [68]) as discussed below.

sec.title: REGULATION OF GATA4 ACTIVATION BY PROTEIN PHOSPHORYLATION
sec.p: Evidence suggests that the activation of GATA factors is regulated by protein phosphorylation. Crossley & Orkin (1994 [69]) reported that GATA1 is phosphorylated at serine residues in the N-terminal region. GATA2 was found to be phosphorylated by extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERK) in response to interleukin signals (Towatari et al., 1995 [70]). GATA4 can be phosphorylated in response to hypertrophic stimuli such as phenylephrine (Morimoto et al., 2000 [18]) and endothelin-1 (Kitta et al., 2001 [71]) in cardiac myocytes at serine 105 (Liang et al., 2001 [72]; Kitta et al., 2003 [40]). p38 MAPK has also been shown to phosphorylate GATA4 at serine 105 (Kerkela et al., 2002 [73]; Charron et al., 2001 [74]). Both ERK and p38 MAPK were found to mediate the wall stress-induced activation of GATA4 binding in adult rat left ventricle (Tenhunen et al., 2004 [75]). In isolated rat atria, p38 MAPK-dependent GATA4 phosphorylation mediates hypertrophic responses (Kerkela et al., 2011 [76]). GATA4 that is phosphorylated at this site is more resistant to cellular degradation (Suzuki, 2003 [47]).

The RhoA/Rho kinase (ROCK) pathway has been show to be upstream of GATA4 phosphorylation by ERK and p38 MAPK in cardiac myocytes (Charron et al., 2001 [74]); Yanazume et al., 2002 [77]). In pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells, we have shown that the 5-HT signal for the nuclear translocation of ERK and GATA4 phosphorylation is dependent on the activation of RhoA and ROCK (Liu et al., 2004 [78]).

Some studies suggest that PI-3 kinase/Akt/GSK pathway regulates GATA4. Sadoshima and co-workers reported that glycogen synthase kinase3 (GSK3)-β regulates subcellular localization of GATA4 and beta-adrenergic receptor stimulation induces GSK3-β phosphorylation/inactivation followed by nuclear accumulation of GATA4 (Morisco et al., 2001 [79]). Subsequent studies have shown that Akt induces hypertrophy in vivo by activating the glycogen synthase kinase3-beta/GATA 4 pathway (Condorelli et al., 2002 [80]) and the deletion of GSK-3beta in mice was found to increase nuclear GATA4 and promote cardiac hypertrophy (Kerkela et al., 2008 [81]). IL-18 induced ANF gene transcription and hypertrophy of neonatal rat ventricular myocytes via the PI-3 kinase/Akt/GATA4 pathway (Chandrasekar et al., 2005 [82]). Naito et al. (2003 [83]) reported that PI3-kinase inhibition suppressed the GATA4 expression.

GATA4 has also been shown to be phosphorylated by protein kinase A. Tremblay et al. (2002 [84]) showed that cAMP stimulation of gonadal cells leads to phosphorylation of GATA4. Further studies by this group identified conserved serine 261 in the GATA4 molecule to be phosphorylated by protein kinase A (Tremblay & Viger, 2003 [85]).

sec.title: REGULATION OF GATA4 BY LYSINE MODIFICATIONS
sec.p: Lysine can be modified via acetylation, sumoylation and ubiquitination (Freiman & Tjian, 2003 [86]) and GATA factors are also subjected to these modifications. In 1998, Boyes et al. (1998 [87]) reported that GATA1 is acetylated. GATA2 (Hayakawa et al., 2004 [88]) and GATA3 (Yamagata et al., 2000 [89]) have also been shown to be acetylated.

Yanazume et al. (2003 [90]) reported that stimulation of neonatal rat cardiac myocytes with phenylephrine increased an acetylated form of GATA4. A dominant-negative mutant of p300 suppressed phenylephrine-induced GATA4 acetylation as well as hypertrophic responses. In contrast to the activation of MEK which phosphorylates GATA4 and causes compensated concentric hypertrophy as described above, overexpression of p300 promoted eccentric dilatation and systolic dysfunction, suggesting the role of acetylated GATA4 in decompensated heart failure. More recently, curcumin, which possesses the histone acetyltransferase inhibitory activity, was found to inhibit acetylation of GATA4 and prevent heart failure (Morimoto et al., 2008 [91]). GATA4 acetylation also plays a role in the differentiation of embryonic stem cells into cardiac myocytes (Kawamura et al., 2005 [92]).

Acetylation sites have been identified to be Lys-311, Lys-318, Lys-320, and Lys-322 (Takaya et al., 2008 [93]). Cdk9 kinase activity was required for the p300-induced transcriptional activities, DNA binding, and acetylation of GATA4 (Sunagawa et al., 2010 [94]). Histone deacetylase 2 (HDAC2) and a small homeodomain factor, Hopx mediate deacetylation of GATA4 (Trivedi et al., 2010 [95]). Our laboratory has shown that acetylated GATA4 is more resistance to degradation, perhaps due to blocking ubiquitination which also occurs on lysine residues (Suzuki et al., 2004 [48]).

GATA4 contains putative sumoylation site at Lysine 366. This site was found to be sumoylated by small ubiquitin-like modifier-1 (SUMO-1) (Komatsu et al., 2004 [96]; Wang et al., 2004 [97]). Sumoylation resulted in enhanced GATA4 activity. Mutation of lysine 366 to arginine indicated that sumoylation regulates nuclear localization of GATA4 (Wang et al., 2004 [97]).

sec.title: REGULATION OF GATA4 GENE EXPRESSION
sec.p: The GATA4 activity can be enhanced by increasing the expression of GATA4 protein. In cultured neonatal cardiac myocytes, electrical pacing-induced hypertrophy is associated with an increase in GATA4 mRNA (Xia et al., 2000 [98]). In rats, pulmonary artery banding (Bar et al., 2003 [99]) and hypoxic pulmonary hypertension (Park et al., 2010 [100]) have been shown to increase GATA4 gene expression in the right ventricle. The treatment of mice with acute intermittent hypoxia also increased GATA4 mRNA and protein expression in the heart (Park et al., 2007 [101]). Increased GATA4 expression was associated with the enhancement of GATA4 DNA binding activity (Park et al., 2010 [100]; Park et al., 2007 [101]).

To understand regulatory mechanisms of the induction of GATA4 expression, our laboratory identified the transcriptional start site of the Gata4 gene and found a regulatory region in its promoter. We performed 5′-Rapid Amplification of cDNA Ends (5′-RACE) analysis to identify the transcriptional start site of the Gata4 gene (Suzuki et al., 2004 [48]; Park et al., 2007 [101]; Nagase et al., 2006 [102]; Suzuki et al., 2007 [103]). We found that 5′ mRNA end occurs 0.6 kb upstream of the ATG translational start site, with 3.5 kb intron existing 0.5 kb upstream of the ATG site as indicated in Fig. 2 (Park et al., 2007 [101]; Nagase et al., 2006 [102]; Suzuki et al., 2007 [103]). The 1,000 bp region immediately upstream from the identified transcriptional start site is conserved and shares 90% homology with the promoter of the rat Gata4 gene. Similar results were reported by Ohara et al. (2006 [104]). We found that the 250 bp region proximal to the transcriptional start site is important for regulating gene transcription in cardiac muscle cells (Park et al., 2007 [101]). This region contains functionally important CCAAT box, and the DNA binding protein was identified as CCAAT-binding factor (CBF)/nuclear factor-Y (NF-Y) (Park et al., 2010 [100]; Park et al., 2011 [105]).

It has been reported that, in the left ventricle, pressure overload by aortic banding activates GATA4 via post-translational modifications without increasing GATA4 gene expression (Hautala et al., 2001 [19]); while pulmonary artery banding increased GATA4 gene expression in the right ventricle (Bar et al., 2003 [99]). These results suggest that the right ventricle specifically possesses transcriptional mechanism for GATA4 activation. Using the hypoxic pulmonary hypertension model of right ventricular hypertrophy, we found that CBF/NF-Y activation occurs through the liberation from a complex with annexin A1 protein via reactive oxygen species-mediated degradation of annexin A1 (Fig. 3; Park et al., 2010 [100]). One difference between left and right ventricles is that the right ventricle has a higher CBF/NF-Y to annexin A1 ratio, compared to the left ventricle, thereby making more efficient for the CBF/NF-Y activation upon the annexin A1 degradation (Park et al., 2010 [100]).

In addition to the regulation at the transcriptional level, Sharma et al. (2007 [68]) reported that GATA4 expression is regulated at the translational level. Authors found that the GATA4 mRNA 5′-UTR contains internal ribosome entry site (IRES) activity that is stimulated during hypertrophic responses induced by vasopressin in cardiac myocytes. This translational activity is regulated by sarcoplasmic reticular calcium as well as protein kinase C.

sec.title: NEGATIVE REGULATION OF GATA4 GENE EXPRESSION
sec.p: As described above, various apoptotic agents such as anthracyclines, nitric oxide and ischemia/reperfusion have been shown to downregulate GATA4 expression. Our previous study has shown that the inhibition of general gene transcription by actinomycin D did not alter the rate of downregulation of Gata4 mRNA promoted by anthracyclines, suggesting that the mRNA stability was not affected. Cloning of the Gata4 promoter allowed for testing if this negative regulation is transcriptionally regulated. Our studies using cloned 250 bp proximal region of the Gata4 promoter revealed that daunorubicin inhibits the binding activity of CBF/NF-Y to CCAAT box in cardiac muscle cells (Park et al., 2011 [105]). We further found that daunorubicin promotes nuclear translocation of p53 and elicit protein-protein interactions between p53 and CBF/NF-Y to suppress the DNA binding activity (Park et al., 2011 [105]; Fig. 4).

Nitric oxide also signals to suppress Gata4 gene expression. In cardiac muscle cells, nitric oxide-mediated downregulation of Gata4 is dependent on protein kinase G (Suzuki et al., 2004 [96]). In contrast, nitric oxide-mediated Gata4 downregulation appears to be independent of protein kinase G (Suzuki et al., 2009 [106]), but regulated by Egr1 in pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells (Suzuki et al., 2007 [103]).

sec.title: GATA4 ACTIVATION BY REDOX SIGNALING
sec.p: Evidence suggests that cell signaling for GATA4 activation is sensitive to antioxidant inhibition. The actions of antioxidants may be due to inhibiting reactive oxygen species (ROS) that serve as second messengers (Suzuki et al., 1997 [107]) or via mechanisms independent of ROS.

In pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells, GATA4 activation has been shown to depend on ROS signaling. The major GATA factor of smooth muscle cells in systemic circulation is GATA6 and mitogens have been shown to downregulate GATA6 which suppresses cell cycle proteins (Perlman et al., 1998 [108]; Mano et al., 1999 [109]). Thus, we initially hypothesized that an important mediator of pulmonary hypertension, serotonin (5-HT), promotes the growth of pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells by downregulating GATA6. However, in pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells, we found that GATA4 is expressed and its DNA binding activity is enhanced by 5-HT (Suzuki et al., 2003 [110]). 5-HT-mediated activation of GATA4 is through reactive oxygen species and MEK/ERK-dependent phosphorylation at serine 105 (Suzuki et al., 2003 [110]). Subsequently, we have shown that the 5-HT signal for the nuclear translocation of ERK and GATA4 phosphorylation is dependent on the activation of RhoA and Rho kinase (Liu et al., 2004 [78]). Rabinovitch and co-workers also showed that GATA4 is phosphorylated and activated via ERK in response to ROS generation by 5-HT (Lawrie et al., 2005 [111]). They proposed that ROS promote the translocation of ERK to the nucleus. We recently found that Rho guanine nucleotide dissociation inhibitor (RhoGDI), which functions to prevent the exchange of GTP for GDP on the Rho-GTPases by guanine nucleotide exchange factors, is carbonylated in response to 5-HT (Wong et al., 2010 [112]). Thus, carbonylation of RhoGDI may trigger RhoA/Rho kinase activation, leading to the nuclear translocation of ERK and GATA4 phosphorylation. Fig. 5 depicts proposed ROS-dependent cell signaling pathways for GATA4 activation in pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells. Also, in cardiac myocytes, as described above, membrane depolarization activates calcium-dependent signaling for GATA4 only when the cells are pretreated with hydrogen peroxide (Morad & Suzuki, 2000 [64]). These results are consistent with the idea that GATA4 is an oxidative stress responsive transcription factor (Suzuki, 2003 [47]).

Antioxidant inhibitable step of signal transduction (Suzuki et al., 1994 [113]) for GATA4 activation has also been reported (Kitta et al., 2001 [114]). In HL-1 cardiac muscle cells, an antioxidant N-acetylcysteine was found to inhibit hepatocyte growth factor (HGF)-induced GATA4 phosphorylation, suggesting the role of ROS. However, this was due to a shift in kinetics of GATA4 phosphorylation via ROS independent mechanism (Kitta et al., 2001 [114]). The PMA-induced ERK/GATA4 pathway was inhibited by α-tocopherol (vitamin E) in pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells, but not in cardiac muscle cells (Clement et al., 2002 [115]).

sec.title: CONCLUSIONS
sec.p: GATA4 plays important roles in gene transcription of various genes in various tissues. Specific actions of GATA4 to regulate these genes under different situations are likely regulated by activating differential cell signaling pathways. As described in the present article, GATA4 can be activated through increasing the activity of the already existing GATA4 protein molecule or by increasing the GATA4 protein expression. Post-translational modifications of GATA4 includes protein-protein interactions, protein phosphorylation by kinases such as ERK, p38 MAPK, PKA and GSK, protein acetylation, and protein sumoylation. GATA4 protein expression can be altered through transcriptional or translational mechanisms. Identifications of molecular mechanisms of cell signaling for GATA4 modulation should contribute to developing therapeutic strategies to treat various diseases in which GATA4 has been implicated.

caption.title: Proposed calcium signaling pathways for GATA4-dependent gene transcription in the heart
caption.p: Normal cardiac muscle contraction is dependent on fast and transient kinetics of calcium release. Ligand activation by hypertrophic stimuli such as angiotensin II and alpha-agonists as well as redox modulations of the ryanodine receptor may activate slow and sustained calcium release that is sensed by calmodulin. Calcium-calmodulin, in turn, activates calcineurin that dephosphorylates NFAT. Dephosphorylated and active NFAT gets translocated into the nucleus, and interacts with GATA4, triggering gene transcription.

caption.title: Gata4 gene regulatory regions
caption.p: Transcriptional start site of the Gata4 gene occurs 4.1 kb upstream from the translational start site with 3.5kb intron. Regulatory regions reside within 0.25 kb upstream from the transcriptional start site.

caption.title: Proposed cell signaling pathways for the activation of Gata4 gene transcription
caption.p: CCAAT box plays an important role in the transcription of the Gata4 gene and is regulated by CBF/NF-Y transcription factor. CBF/NF-Y is inactive when annexin A1 is bound. Signaling stimuli liberate CBF/NF-Y as an active form via the production of ROS, which in turn carbonylate annexin A1. Carbonylated annexin A1 gets degraded by proteasomes.

caption.title: A proposed mechanism for inhibition of Gata4 gene transcription by apoptotic stimuli
caption.p: Some apoptotic stimuli increase nuclear p53 that can bind to CBF/NF-Y, inhibiting its DNA binding activity, thereby suppressing Gata4 gene transcription.

caption.title: Proposed ROS-dependent signaling pathways for GATA4 activation
caption.p: Signaling stimuli trigger the generation of ROS, which in turn (i) activate MEK, phosphorylating ERK and (ii) activate RhoA/ROCK pathway, facilitating ERK nuclear translocation. In the nucleus, ERK then phosphorylates and activates GATA4.
